description: We are a team of students interested in AI, data analysis, software development, and space technology. For Flame in Freefall, we aim to build an interactive AI-powered dashboard that analyzes NASA’s microgravity combustion data and presents meaningful fire-safety insights. Our team combines skills in programming, AI/ML, data analysis, visualization, and UI/UX
summary: QUENCH is an interactive evidence tool for spacecraft fire safety, built for the Flame in Freefall challenge. Future Moon cabins may run at 30% oxygen or more, but the solid-fuel flight tests in NASA's PSI archive reach only 22.2% oxygen. QUENCH makes that gap visible. A user picks a cabin atmosphere (ISS, reduced pressure or exploration) and sees which archived NASA flight runs match its oxygen and pressure, split by fuel type: solid materials, liquid droplets and gas flames. The site also ranks 15 findings with adjustable weights, tracks flame spread in raw BASS-II flight video, and includes a droplet-extinction model trained on FLEX data. Every finding is linked to its NASA source and labeled by how it was produced, and limits are stated openly. This matters because crews need fire-response plans backed by evidence for the air they will actually breathe, and QUENCH shows where tests are still missing.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

QUENCH turns NASA's open combustion archive (PSI) into a decision aid. The evidence map plots flight runs by oxygen and pressure, so users can see what has and has not been tested for ISS air, a 10.2 psia reduced-pressure cabin and a 34% oxygen exploration atmosphere. For the exploration cabin, the archive has no matching solid-material runs.

KEY FEATURES

- Cabin coverage and evidence map: matching runs by fuel type, with CSV downloads and column notes.

- 15 ranked findings with filters and adjustable weights (safety impact, strength of evidence, fit to Moon and Mars missions, ability to act now). Each has its evidence, limits, sources and a suggested action.

- Recommended tests and related investigations (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, LUCI).

- Experiment analysis: a tracker measures flame-front spread in BASS-II flight video, with calibration checks. The Saffire-II comparison shows burn lengths in microgravity and on Earth, sample by sample.

- FLEX droplet extinction model, trained on 261 FLEX runs to predict whether a droplet flame goes out. In cross-validation by test day it reached 82% accuracy, against 69% for always predicting the most common outcome. It warns users when they are extrapolating outside tested conditions.

- Ask the archive: a question box (English or Russian). Each answer is labeled as written by Claude or taken from archive excerpts from challenge organizer resources. Cosmo, our archive companion, guides users.

HOW IT WORKS

Statistics are recomputed from archived PSI tables. The build checks cited numbers and selected quotations against their sources. Each finding is labeled by how it was produced: computed from run tables, NASA record, archive audit, measured from video, or model.

BENEFIT AND INTENDED IMPACT

Mission planners and researchers can quickly see where evidence is missing and which tests to prioritise, such as partial-gravity and exploration-atmosphere experiments. The goal is evidence-based fire safety for crews beyond Earth.

TOOLS

- Front end: hand-written static website (HTML, CSS, JavaScript).

- Data and analysis: [Python / libraries used] for cleaning NASA PSI data, the flame-front tracker and the FLEX model.

- Ask feature: [backend or serverless function] calling the Claude API.

- Data sources: NASA PSI archive and NASA Glenn resources.

- AI use, disclosed: Claude (Anthropic) assisted with code, data normalisation, draft summaries and findings. OpenAI Codex assisted with the interface redesign. OpenAI image generation was used for the QUENCH logo and Cosmo. NASA photographs are credited to their sources.

CREATIVITY

We combine an interactive evidence map, automatic analysis of raw flight video, a validated predictive model and transparent limits in one tool, so a non-expert can see the gap in minutes.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Honesty about what the data cannot show (different pressures, missing combustion outcomes, extrapolation), reproducibility through open downloads, and clear labeling of all AI-generated or AI-assisted content.
